name: Text to SQL Benchmarks
title: Text to SQL Benchmarks
answer: Text to SQL benchmarks are standard test sets that measure how well a system turns a plain language question into a working SQL query. Public benchmarks such as Spider and BIRD score systems by running the generated query and comparing its result with a known correct answer. Enterprise schemas are larger and less tidy than the benchmarks, so real accuracy is usually lower. The topic sits inside AI and SQL, alongside the wider tooling that connects models to databases.

sections.body: Text to SQL benchmarks are standard test sets that measure how well a system turns a plain language question into a working SQL query. Public benchmarks such as Spider and BIRD score systems by running the generated query and comparing its result with a known correct answer. Enterprise schemas are larger and less tidy than the benchmarks, so real accuracy is usually lower. The topic sits inside AI and SQL, alongside the wider tooling that connects models to databases.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Running a benchmark means holding a database, a set of questions, and a set of reference queries or answers, then executing each generated query against the database. The work is mostly ordinary database infrastructure: a PostgreSQL or similar instance, a harness that submits queries and captures results, and a scoring script that compares outcomes. The site itself is built from a PostgreSQL database, which is the same engine many of these benchmarks use. Some harnesses now reach the database through a Model Context Protocol server, and this site tracks 263 such servers for SQL databases and warehouses out of 2526 active ones.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The usual method is execution accuracy: run the generated query, take its result set, and check it against the result of the reference query, so different but equivalent SQL can still pass. Exact match scoring, which compares query text, is cheaper but punishes valid rewrites. Harder variants add noisy schemas, ambiguous questions, and multi table joins, and BIRD in particular includes external evidence alongside the question. Results are reported per difficulty band, and error analysis usually separates wrong schema linking from wrong joins, wrong filters, and wrong aggregation.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Benchmark data carries its own rights questions, since schemas, questions, and reference queries are published artifacts with licences and citation expectations. Provenance matters for reproducibility: the database version, the split used, and the scoring script all affect the number reported, so a score without that context is hard to trust. When benchmarks are reused for evaluation of commercial systems, teams need to know whether the test set leaked into training data, which inflates results. The site library holds 319 research papers, and many of the benchmark papers sit there with their own terms of use.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward benchmarks that look more like real deployments: bigger schemas, messier column names, business definitions, and questions that need clarification before any SQL is written. Evaluation is also moving from single queries toward multi step tasks, including query repair and dialogue, and toward agent style setups where a model inspects the schema before answering. As text to SQL moves into production, benchmark scores will matter less on their own and more as one input alongside task specific tests on a team's own data. The field remains a measurement problem as much as a modelling one.
